text_blocks.snippet: Influenza A and B are two types of influenza viruses that cause seasonal flu, but they have some key differences. Influenza A is generally more common and can infect both humans and animals, potentially leading to pandemics. Influenza B primarily infects humans and tends to cause milder symptoms, although it can still be severe in some cases, particularly in young children.
snippet_highlighted_words: Influenza A is generally more common and can infect both humans and animals, potentially leading to pandemics.
Influenza B primarily infects humans and tends to cause milder symptoms, although it can still be severe in some cases, particularly in young children

list.title: More common and widespread:
list.snippet: Flu A is the most frequently identified type during flu seasons, according to the CDC.

list.title: Animal Reservoir:
list.snippet: Flu A viruses can infect various animal species, including birds and pigs, making it more prone to genetic mutation and potentially leading to new strains.

list.title: Pandemic Potential:
list.snippet: Because of its ability to jump between species and mutate, Flu A has the potential to cause pandemics, as seen with past outbreaks like the Spanish Flu.

list.title: Generally causes more severe illness:
list.snippet: While symptoms can vary, Flu A infections are often more severe than Flu B, with a higher likelihood of hospitalization and complications, particularly in older adults and those with underlying health conditions, according to the CDC.

list.title: Primarily human-specific:
list.snippet: Unlike Flu A, Flu B primarily infects humans and does not have a significant animal reservoir.

list.title: Generally milder symptoms:
list.snippet: Flu B infections tend to be less severe than Flu A, with milder symptoms and a lower risk of complications, though it can still cause serious illness in vulnerable populations.

list.title: Can cause outbreaks:
list.snippet: While less common than Flu A, Flu B can still cause seasonal outbreaks, especially in children and older adults.

list.title: Less likely to mutate:
list.snippet: Because it doesn't have an animal reservoir, Flu B tends to mutate more slowly than Flu A, making it less prone to causing pandemics.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Both Flu A and Flu B can cause similar symptoms, including fever, cough, sore throat, muscle aches, fatigue, and headache.

list.title: Transmission:
list.snippet: Both viruses spread through respiratory droplets produced when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: The treatment for both Flu A and Flu B is generally the same, including rest, fluids, and over-the-counter medications for symptom relief, with antiviral medications available for severe cases.

list.title: Prevention:
list.snippet: Both can be prevented through vaccination, practicing good hygiene (handwashing, covering coughs and sneezes), and avoiding close contact with sick individuals.

text_blocks.snippet: Flu A and Flu B are two types of influenza viruses that cause seasonal flu. While they share similar symptoms, Flu A is more common, more likely to mutate, and can cause more severe illness, especially in adults, while Flu B is more common in children. Both are spread through respiratory droplets and can be treated with similar methods, including rest, fluids, and sometimes antiviral medications.

Host Range: Can infect humans, pigs, and birds.
Circulation: Tends to circulate most during the fall and winter months.
Commonality: Accounts for about 25% of flu cases.
